node.label: Joan Sangster
node.date_label: Dreams of Equality (1989) · “Beyond Dichotomies” (1995) · “Feminism and the Making of Canadian Working-Class History” (2000) · Through Feminist Eyes: collection and retrospective introduction (2011)
node.description: A Canadian historian who brings feminist questions to labour history and treats the relationship between women’s history, gender analysis and class as an argument to be worked through. Her 2000 essay examines feminist challenges to a labour narrative centred on men and asks how race, ethnicity and gender change class formation. In her 2011 retrospective she explains that the 1995–96 exchange opposed a hierarchy that treated gender history as necessarily superior to women’s history. The entry preserves the difference between this retrospective and the original interventions.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Dreams of Equality (1989); “Beyond Dichotomies” (1995); “Reconsidering Dichotomies” (1996); “Feminism and the Making of Canadian Working-Class History” (2000); Through Feminist Eyes (2011; collection with a new retrospective introduction).
node.scope_note: Existing scoped primary readings and the author’s later introduction are reused honestly; no new reading of Dreams of Equality, Regulating Girls and Women or Girl Trouble is claimed. The existing jointly authored 1992 reply to Bliss remains a separate intervention and is not recast as a reply to Granatstein’s 1998 book. No generic mentor or affiliation arrows.

proposed_edges.relationship: Uses feminist critiques to reconsider gender, race and ethnicity within accounts of working-class formation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Reuse of the recorded abstract and bounded 2000 essay readings. The field’s masculinist starting points are Sangster’s diagnosis. This does not infer a single causal genealogy from political organizing.

proposed_edges.relationship: Questions treating women’s history and gender history as opposed stages in an inevitable methodological succession.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The 2011 introduction’s own retrospect supports this formulation; existing addenda separately record full readings of the two original essays. The disagreement and Sangster’s concessions remain situated, not an assertion that all gender historians held one position.
